title: Circuits & Electronics for Scientists
subject: Circuits & Electronics
summary: A hands-on, intuition-first introduction to circuits and electronics for a chemist who works with NMR, ICP-MS, potentiostats and other detectors, designed to run alongside the algebra and precalculus refresher (M0): it uses only algebra, exponentials and logarithms, and trigonometry, with complex-number phasors, and flags where calculus will later deepen each idea. Seven units cover charge, current, voltage and power; DC analysis (dividers, Kirchhoff, nodal and mesh analysis as linear systems); Thevenin equivalents, meters, grounding, safety and the Wheatstone bridge; capacitors, inductors and the RC time constant; AC, impedance, filters and resonance; diodes, transistors and op-amps including the transimpedance amplifier; and instrumentation (ADC and DAC, noise, the potentiostat, NMR and mass-spectrometer signal chains). Schematic reading, back-of-envelope estimates and 'why does the physics work this way' come before calculation.

units.title: Charge, Current, Voltage and Power
units.summary: The vocabulary of every circuit: current as charge flow (and moles of electrons, via Faraday's constant), voltage as energy per charge (the same quantity as electrochemical cell potential), resistance and Ohm's law, and how to read a resistor and a schematic. Water analogies are used and then deliberately broken.

lessons.title: Charge, Current and the Water Analogy
objectives: Define current as charge per time, I = ΔQ/Δt, and convert among amperes, coulombs per second, electrons per second and moles of electrons per second (n = It/F), including the sign convention that I points the way positive charge would move.
Use I = nqAv_d to see that electron drift speed in a wire is only tenths of a millimetre per second, and explain why a lamp nevertheless lights at once.

Map the water-pipe analogy (flow rate, pressure, pipe) onto current, voltage and wire, and name two places the analogy misleads (charge cannot spill out of a cut wire; the signal travels in the field, not by carriers pushing along the wire).

objectives: Explain voltage as energy per unit charge (1 V = 1 J/C), why it is always a difference between two points, and how it is the same quantity as a cell potential in ΔG = −nFE.
Compute power P = IV and energy E = Pt, converting between joules, watt-hours and battery ratings in mAh.
Use the passive sign convention to decide whether a component is absorbing or supplying power.

Compute R = ρL/A for a wire or a conductivity cell, and predict how R changes when length, area or material changes; relate resistivity to conductivity as used in solution conductivity meters.
Explain why the resistance of a metal rises with temperature while that of a semiconductor or an electrolyte falls.

units.title: Series, Parallel and Kirchhoff: DC Circuit Analysis
units.summary: From combining resistors to solving any resistor network: series and parallel reduction, voltage and current dividers, Kirchhoff's two conservation laws, and nodal and mesh analysis written as systems of linear equations (the elimination skills from M0's systems-of-equations lessons).

lessons.title: Series and Parallel Resistors
objectives: Compute equivalent resistance for series and parallel combinations, and justify each rule from 'same current' (series) and 'same voltage' (parallel), with conductances adding in parallel.
Reduce a mixed network step by step to one equivalent resistor, and check the answer by power conservation.

lessons.title: Voltage and Current Dividers
objectives: Derive and use V_out = V_in R_2/(R_1+R_2) and the current divider I_1 = I R_2/(R_1+R_2), explaining why the other branch's resistor sits in the numerator.
Predict how a load connected across the output of a divider changes V_out, and state the rule of thumb for when the load can be ignored (load ≫ R_2).
Recognise dividers in real hardware: potentiometers, sensor read-outs such as a thermistor or photoresistor, and attenuator probes.

lessons.title: Kirchhoff's Laws
objectives: State Kirchhoff's current law as conservation of charge at a node and the voltage law as conservation of energy around a loop (a charge returning to its start has no net energy change).
Apply both laws to a circuit with consistent sign conventions to find all branch currents in a one-source, two-loop network.
Verify a solution by checking that power supplied equals power absorbed.

objectives: Write Kirchhoff's current law at each non-reference node as a matrix equation G V = I and solve a two- or three-node network by elimination or substitution (the linear-systems toolkit from M0).
Explain why a reference node is needed, why N nodes give N−1 independent equations, and why the conductance matrix is symmetric for resistor networks.
Interpret the diagonal entry of G as the total conductance at a node and the off-diagonal entries as minus the conductance connecting two nodes.

units.title: Equivalent Circuits and Measurement
units.summary: Thevenin and Norton equivalents and maximum power transfer, then the practical lab questions they answer: what a meter does to the circuit it measures, why mains hum gets into signals and how ground and shielding fight it, electrical safety, and the Wheatstone bridge behind conductivity, strain and thermal-conductivity sensors.

lessons.title: Thevenin and Norton Equivalents
objectives: Reduce any two-terminal linear network to a Thevenin equivalent (V_th = open-circuit voltage, R_th = V_oc/I_sc, or R_th with sources turned off) and convert to the Norton form with I_N = V_th/R_th.
Model a real source (battery, function generator, electrode) as an ideal source plus an internal resistance, and predict its terminal voltage under load.
Explain what the equivalent preserves (behaviour at the terminals) and what it does not (heat dissipated inside).

lessons.title: Maximum Power Transfer and Matching
objectives: Show with algebra (no calculus) that power in the load, P_L = V_th²R_L/(R_th+R_L)², is largest at R_L = R_th, using (R_th − R_L)² ≥ 0, and that P_max = V_th²/(4R_th) at 50% efficiency.
Decide when matching is wanted (RF and signal chains, 50 Ω systems) and when it is the opposite of what you want (power distribution, voltmeters, low-loss supplies).
demoIdeas: Plot load power and efficiency against R_L/R_th on a log axis: the power peak sits at 1, efficiency passes through 50% there.

lessons.title: Meters, Loading and Internal Resistance
objectives: Explain why a voltmeter (high input resistance, in parallel) and an ammeter (low resistance, in series) disturb the circuit they measure, and compute the loading error using a Thevenin model of the circuit.
Explain why a high-impedance source such as a pH glass electrode (~100 MΩ) needs an electrometer or buffer rather than a 10 MΩ multimeter.
Explain why a four-wire (Kelvin) measurement of a small resistance removes lead and contact resistance.

lessons.title: Ground, Shielding and Electrical Safety
objectives: Distinguish circuit ground (a reference node), chassis/earth ground and a ground loop, and explain how mains hum couples in capacitively and inductively and how shielding, twisted pairs, coax and single-point grounding reduce it.
Explain that current through the body, not voltage alone, determines harm (about 1 mA perceptible, 10–20 mA can't let go, ~100 mA risks fibrillation), and estimate it from V/R_body.
State basic lab safety practice: never defeat a ground pin, treat charged capacitors and high-voltage supplies (as in MS and ICP-MS) as live, use one hand when probing, and know what a GFCI trips on.

lessons.title: The Wheatstone Bridge
objectives: Derive the balance condition R_1/R_2 = R_3/R_x and explain why a null measurement is insensitive to the source voltage and to the detector's calibration.
Compute the small output voltage of a bridge with one varying arm, V_out ≈ V_s ΔR/(4R), and explain why a bridge beats a plain divider for small changes.
Name sensor uses: strain gauges, thermistors, thermal-conductivity and Pirani detectors, and AC conductivity-cell bridges.

units.title: Capacitors, Inductors and Time Constants
units.summary: What a capacitor and an inductor physically are, why one resists changes in voltage and the other changes in current, and how that gives the exponential charging curve with its time constant (algebra and exponentials only; the calculus behind it is flagged for later). Chemistry hooks: the electrode double layer and T1 relaxation follow the same curve.

lessons.title: Capacitors: Storing Charge and Energy
objectives: Explain C = Q/V physically, use the parallel-plate result C = ε₀ε_r A/d to predict what a dielectric or a change of spacing does, and compute stored energy U = ½CV².
Combine capacitors in series and in parallel (the reverse of resistors) and say why.
Explain why the current through an ideal capacitor is I = C ΔV/Δt (zero for steady DC, large for a fast change) and relate it to the electrochemical double layer (~10–20 µF/cm²).

lessons.title: Inductors: Magnetic Energy and Inductive Kick
objectives: Explain an inductor as a coil whose magnetic field stores energy U = ½LI² and which opposes changes in current, V = L ΔI/Δt, and give the solenoid result L = μ₀N²A/ℓ and how L scales with turns and size.

Contrast capacitor and inductor (a capacitor resists changes in voltage, an inductor changes in current) and predict the large voltage spike when a coil's current is interrupted; say why flyback diodes and spark suppression exist.

lessons.title: RC and RL Transients: the Time Constant
objectives: Describe RC charging V_C = V_s(1 − e^{−t/τ}) and discharge V_C = V_0 e^{−t/τ} with τ = RC, using the exponential function from M0, and quote the 63%, 86%, 95% and 99% marks at 1τ, 2τ, 3τ and 5τ.

Explain why the curve is exponential: the current through R is proportional to the voltage still to be gained, so the rate of change is proportional to what is left (the same law as first-order kinetics); say where calculus will later turn this into dV/dt = (V_s − V)/RC.
Apply the same shape to an RL circuit (τ = L/R) and to analogues in the lab: electrode double-layer charging, ADC input settling, and T1 relaxation in NMR.

units.title: AC Circuits, Impedance and Resonance
units.summary: Sinusoids, RMS and phase, then phasors as complex-number algebra (M0's complex-number lessons), impedance as Ohm's law for AC, filters as frequency-dependent voltage dividers, and RLC resonance, with the NMR probe's tuned circuit as the running chemistry example. Calculus will later show why a derivative becomes multiplication by jω.

lessons.title: Sinusoids, RMS and Phase
objectives: Describe v(t) = V_p sin(2πft + φ) by amplitude, peak-to-peak, frequency, period and phase, and read the phase from a time delay on a two-channel scope, φ = 360°·Δt/T.
Explain why V_rms = V_p/√2 for a sine (the DC value giving the same heating) and why an AC waveform with zero average still delivers power.
Convert between mains figures (e.g. 120 V rms ≈ 170 V peak ≈ 340 V peak-to-peak).

lessons.title: Phasors: Sinusoids as Complex Numbers

Add two same-frequency sinusoids by adding their phasors, and explain why the amplitudes alone do not add.
Explain that multiplying by j rotates a phasor by +90°, which is the origin of the 90° phase shifts in capacitors and inductors.

Use V = IZ with the series, parallel and divider rules for complex Z, and compute |Z| and the phase for an RC or RL series circuit at a given frequency.
Explain why an ideal capacitor or inductor dissipates no average power although current flows.

lessons.title: Filters: Voltage Dividers that Depend on Frequency
objectives: Treat an RC circuit as a voltage divider with Z_C in place of a resistor and derive the low-pass gain |H| = 1/√(1+(f/f_c)²) with f_c = 1/(2πRC), the −3 dB point and the −20 dB per decade roll-off; swap R and C for a high-pass.

Relate cut-off frequency to the time constant (f_c = 1/(2πτ)) and explain the trade-off: a narrower filter cuts noise but slows the response (rise time ≈ 0.35/f_c).

units.title: Semiconductors and Op-Amps
units.summary: Diodes, LEDs and rectifiers (the exponential I–V is a Boltzmann factor), transistors as switches and amplifiers, and then the op-amp as the universal building block of analogue instruments, ending with the transimpedance amplifier that turns a photodiode, PMT or electrochemical current into a voltage.

lessons.title: Diodes, LEDs and Rectifiers
objectives: Describe the p–n junction qualitatively (depletion region, forward voltage ≈ 0.6–0.7 V for Si, band-gap-set for LEDs) and use the Shockley equation I = I_s(e^{V/V_T} − 1), V_T = kT/q ≈ 25.7 mV, to see why current rises about tenfold per ~60 mV; note the link to the Boltzmann factor.
Size an LED series resistor, R = (V_s − V_f)/I.
Explain a half-wave and bridge rectifier with a smoothing capacitor and estimate the ripple, ΔV ≈ I/(fC).

Design a transistor switch: choose the base resistor to saturate the device and drive an LED or relay, with a flyback diode on inductive loads.
Estimate the gain of a common-emitter amplifier, A_v ≈ −R_C/r_e with r_e ≈ 25 mV/I_E, and explain the inversion and the need for a bias point.

units.title: Instrumentation: From Signal to Number
units.summary: How the pieces combine into the instruments in the lab: ADC and DAC resolution, noise and averaging, the potentiostat block diagram, and the signal chains of an NMR receiver and a mass-spectrometer detector. Each lesson re-uses dividers, RC filters, resonance and op-amps from earlier units.

lessons.title: ADC and DAC: Resolution, Aliasing and Ladders
objectives: Compute the ADC step LSB = V_FS/2^N, the quantisation noise LSB/√12 and the ideal dynamic range (6.02N + 1.76 dB), and explain why a signal is amplified to fill the ADC range but not beyond it.
Explain aliasing (f_s > 2f_max) and why an analogue RC anti-alias filter must come before the converter.
Show how an R-2R ladder DAC builds V_ref × code/2^N from resistor dividers.

lessons.title: Noise: Thermal, Shot, Averaging and Lock-in
objectives: Compute Johnson–Nyquist noise v_n = √(4k_BTRΔf) and shot noise i_n = √(2qIΔf), and say which one limits a high-R sensor and which one limits a photocurrent.
Explain why averaging N scans improves SNR as √N (signal adds coherently, random noise adds in quadrature), as in NMR scan accumulation, and why narrowing bandwidth reduces noise as √Δf.
Describe the lock-in idea: modulate the signal to a quiet frequency, away from 1/f noise and mains, and detect only a narrow band around it.

Trace a cyclic-voltammetry scan through the blocks (DAC makes the triangle, TIA output goes to the ADC) and estimate the uncompensated iR drop and the double-layer charging time τ = R_uC_dl.
Explain compliance voltage and what limits the current or scan rate a potentiostat can deliver.

Compare pulse-counting and analogue modes in an electron-multiplier ion detector (ICP-MS, MS) and say when each is used and why dead time forces a switch at high count rates.
